newsitem.title: THAILAND: Exiles applaud Burma sanctions, no word from govt.
newsitem.headline: Exiles applaud Burma sanctions, no word from govt.

text.p: Exiled Burmese dissidents on Tuesday applauded a United States decision to impose economic sanctions on Burma, but there was no official comment from the military government in Rangoon.
"Oh great, this is good news. We are very happy," said Aung Naing Oo, foreign affairs secretary for the students group the All Burma Students' Democratic Front (ABSDF).
The ABSDF and other exile groups in Thailand and elsewhere have urged the United States and other governments to stop investing in Burma because of human rights abuses there.

Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has been accused by human rights organisations and many Western governments of abuses, such as summary executions, using forced labour and employing repressive tactics against the opposition.
The SLORC has also been condemned for failing to recognise the elected government of the National League for Democracy (NLD) party co-founded by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.

"Since the SLORC came into power through a bloody military coup in 1988, they have enjoyed assistance from the business community, which has enabled them to consolidate power and accelerate their campaign of terror against the people of Burma," Aung Naing Oo told Reuters.
Burma has approved a total of $6.05 billion in foreign investment since it opened up the economy in 1988. Diplomats say a little over half that has actually been invested.
The United States is the fourth-largest investor in Burma in terms of approved foreign investment.
The U.S. State Department was due to announce economic sanctions on Burma later on Tuesday, an administration official said in Washington.
The sanctions will ban new U.S. investment in Burma. Several American companies have pulled out of the country over the past few years because of pressure by human rights organisations.
Major companies still doing business there include oil companies Unocal Corp and Atlantic Richfield Co.
Unocal, the largest U.S. investor in Burma, said on Tuesday it was disappointed by the sanctions but they would not affect its investment policy in the region.
Attempts to reach Burmese government officials were unsuccessful on Tuesday.
But last week a Burmese government official told Reuters that U.S. sanctions were like a weapon aimed at destroying the human rights of the Burmese people.
Suu Kyi, who served six years of house arrest for outspoken attacks on the military government, could not be reached for comment. Her telephone line appeared to have been cut.
In the past she has urged investors to stay away from Burma and has said she supported the idea of U.S. sanctions.
Diplomats said the sanctions would likely cause U.S. and other investors to be more cautious in coming to Burma.
"They'll have to think a lot harder. Some companies may decide not to come in. It adds political risk," a diplomat said.
Diplomats from member nations in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said the sanctions will not likely affect Burma's efforts to join the seven-member group.
They said ASEAN, which follows a policy of non-interference in the politics of its neighbours, continued to oppose Western intervention in Burma.

"If you isolate a country, it doesn't go the way you want," said one diplomat, noting the U.S. failure to bring down the long-running regime of Fidel Castro in Cuba through a variety of methods, including sanctions.
